extracted.intended_audience: Researchers invited to review (or wishing to review) for Royal Society journals; including early-career researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for researchers who are invited, or who wish to register, to perform peer review for Royal Society journals, including qualifications, ethical expectations, procedures for co-reviewing, anonymity/options for publishing reports, and available recognition/support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be suitably qualified to review
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to be qualified at least PhD level (or equivalent) in a relevant subject, an active researcher and have published recently in one or more reputable peer reviewed journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have less experience, there is still the option to co-review with your supervisor or another colleague. Approach them expressing your interest so if they get invited you can review with them and get recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept invitations when suitably qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are invited to review for one of our journals, and are suitably qualified to review the work, please try to say 'yes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Society will give you recognition (if you want it) and full support. Editors select reviewers based on relevant expertise from a wide and diverse pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register to be considered as a reviewer (ScholarOne)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a journal reviewer, please register on ScholarOne. Once registered you will be considered as a reviewer for manuscripts that are within your research area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are flagged within our system but we cannot guarantee that you will be selected as a reviewer for one of our journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base recommendations on scientific merits; avoid unconscious bias
rubrics_metrics.description: We remind reviewers to be aware of any unconscious biases when assessing a paper... recommendations are based on the scientific merits of a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible biases to be aware of are country of origin, institution, name, gender, race and ethnicity to name a few. The Society and its journals are committed to improving inclusion and diversity within science publishing; reviewers have a vital role to play in this mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewing: role, consent, and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A co-reviewer is defined as a researcher, often early in their career, who reviews a manuscript together with a more senior (invited) reviewer (see co-review policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is the opportunity for the senior reviewer to give recognition to the co-reviewer through the Reviewer Recognition Service and where we publish peer review reports by adding their name (provided consent has been given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity by default with option to sign published reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing in these journals is anonymous by default but reviewers have the option to sign their names to gain recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five journals (Proceedings A, B, Biology Letters, Royal Society Open Science and Open Biology) offer transparency by publishing peer review information (reviewer reports, decision letter and response) under an open access licence (CC-BY 4.0) alongside published articles. Signing is optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use journal-specific reviewer guidelines and concise report forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Each journal has specific reviewer guidelines available via the 'information for...reviewers' menu on each journal homepage. Reviewer report forms are as concise as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarise yourself with the specific journal's guidance and use the concise report form provided to structure your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine supporting data and request assistance if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporting data for articles is easy to access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you require any assistance with your review, contact the Editorial Office of the journal. The Society offers email and telephone support to all reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undertake reviewer training and read guidance on good practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society encourages early-career researchers to get involved in the peer review process and recommends training materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended resources include the Web of Science Academy, Nature Masterclasses, and the Royal Society peer review blog series such as ‘Tips for good practice in peer review’ and ‘What makes a good or a bad peer review?’. New reviewers are recommended to take advantage of training materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and rewards for review work
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society provides recognition for reviewers via multiple mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer rewards include a £200/$254/€233 discount on Article Processing Charges for publishing in fully open access journals; six journals publish annual citable articles listing reviewers who opt in; peer review certificates are available on request; and the Web of Science Reviewer Recognition Service records, verifies and showcases peer review contributions (opt-in via ScholarOne).
